title: Food container employing a cold atmospheric plasma source for prolonged preservation of plant and animal origin food products
author: Dimitrakellis, Giannoglou, et al.

steps.title: Prepare food samples
steps.instruction: Obtain sea bream fillets, fresh‑cut rocket leaves, and whole fresh strawberries to be used as the test food products.

steps.title: Place samples in CAP container
steps.instruction: Arrange the fish fillets, rocket leaves and strawberries inside the cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) food container, ensuring they are positioned for uniform exposure.

steps.title: Apply CAP treatment
steps.instruction: Run the CAP source for 10 min on sea bream fillets and for 15 min on rocket leaves and strawberries.

steps.title: Remove and store samples
steps.instruction: After treatment, take the samples out of the container and store them at refrigeration temperatures (2 °C – 6 °C). For the shelf‑life study, keep sea bream fillets at 4 °C, rocket leaves at 2 °C, and strawberries at 6 °C, alongside untreated control samples.

steps.title: Perform microbiological analysis
steps.instruction: Determine total viable count (TVC) immediately after treatment using the following procedure.

substeps.instruction: Weigh 10 g of each food sample.
Add 90 mL of sterile Ringer solution to the sample.
Homogenize the mixture for 1 min in a sterile plastic bag.
Prepare appropriate serial dilutions and pour‑plate onto Plate Count Agar (PCA).
Count colonies and calculate TVC (log CFU/g).

steps.title: Conduct shelf‑life study
steps.instruction: Monitor quality deterioration of treated and untreated samples during storage and estimate shelf‑life based on the dominant factor for each product.

substeps.instruction: Store the samples at the product‑specific temperatures noted above.
At predetermined time intervals, measure the total microflora for sea bream fillets and rocket leaves, and assess organoleptic attributes together with total phenolic content for strawberries.
Determine the time at which each dominant quality factor exceeds its acceptable limit; this time is the estimated shelf‑life.

Record the observed shelf‑life values (e.g., sea bream fillets: untreated 4 h, CAP‑treated 12 h; rocket leaves: untreated 2 h, CAP‑treated 16 h; strawberries: untreated 23 h, CAP‑treated 36 h) and calculate the percentage extension (≈50 % for fish, >80 % for leaves, ≈40 % for strawberries).
